title: Data Handling
summary: Summarise data with the mean, median, mode, range, quartiles, percentiles and interquartile range, identify outliers, calculate the mean from a frequency table, and draw and interpret scatter plots and broken-line graphs.

notes.text: The **mean** is the sum of the values divided by the number of values; the **median** is the middle value of the **ordered** data; the **mode** is the value that occurs most often. Each summarises the "centre" of the data in a different way.

notes.title: Worked example 1: the mean from a frequency table
notes.problem:
The number of goals a team scored in 15 matches is shown below. Calculate the mean.
Goals: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Number of matches: 3, 5, 4, 2, 1
steps: Multiply each value by its frequency: $0 \times 3 + 1 \times 5 + 2 \times 4 + 3 \times 2 + 4 \times 1 = 0 + 5 + 8 + 6 + 4 = 23$ goals.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Do not divide by the number of rows in the table (5). Divide by the total frequency, the number of matches (15).
Two data sets can have the same mean but very different spreads. **Quartiles** divide the ordered data into four equal parts.

notes.caption: Quartiles and spread
rows: The smallest and largest values (the extremes)
The median of the lower half of the data (25th percentile)
The median of the upper half of the data (75th percentile)
$Q_3 - Q_1$: the spread of the middle 50% of the data

notes.title: Worked example 2: an odd number of values
notes.problem: Find the quartiles, range and IQR of: $3;\ 5;\ 7;\ 8;\ 9;\ 11;\ 13;\ 15;\ 18$
steps: There are 9 values; the median is the 5th: $Q_2 = 9$.
Lower half (values below the median): $3;\ 5;\ 7;\ 8$, so $Q_1 = \dfrac{5 + 7}{2} = 6$.

notes.title: Worked example 3: an even number of values
notes.problem: Find the quartiles and IQR of: $12;\ 15;\ 17;\ 20;\ 22;\ 25;\ 28;\ 30$
steps: Median: halfway between the 4th and 5th values: $\dfrac{20 + 22}{2} = 21$.

notes.text: The $p$th **percentile** is the value below which $p\%$ of the data lies. If your mark is at the 90th percentile, you did better than 90% of the learners. $Q_1$, the median and $Q_3$ are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles.

An **outlier** is a value that is very far from the rest of the data. It may be a mistake, or a genuinely unusual value. Outliers strongly affect the **mean** and the **range**, but hardly affect the median and the IQR.

notes.title: Worked example 4
notes.problem: The ages of learners at a party are $5;\ 6;\ 6;\ 7;\ 8;\ 9$, and one adult aged $40$ is also counted. Compare the mean and median with and without the adult.
steps: The outlier pulls the mean up by almost 5 years but moves the median by only half a year.
notes.answer: The median is the better summary when there is an outlier.

notes.text: A **scatter plot** shows pairs of numerical data as points, to see whether two variables are related. If the points tend to go up from left to right, there is a **positive correlation**; down from left to right is a **negative correlation**; no pattern means **no correlation**.

notes.caption: Scatter plot of hours studied against test mark for 12 learners: a positive correlation.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Correlation does not prove that one thing **causes** the other. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer, but ice cream does not cause drowning; hot weather affects both.
A **broken-line graph** joins data points in time order with straight lines. It is used to show change over time, such as monthly rainfall or a town's population over several years.

items: Mean from a frequency table: $\frac{\text{sum of (value} \times \text{frequency)}}{\text{total frequency}}$.
$Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are the medians of the lower and upper halves; IQR $= Q_3 - Q_1$.
Outliers distort the mean and range; the median and IQR are more resistant.
Scatter plots show positive, negative or no correlation; correlation is not causation.
Broken-line graphs show change over time.

questions.prompt: What does the scatter plot of hours studied against test mark in the notes show?
options: That studying causes high marks for certain
questions.explanation: The points rise from left to right. (A correlation alone does not prove cause.)

questions.prompt: An outlier affects the interquartile range much more than it affects the range.
questions.explanation: The range uses the extreme values, so an outlier changes it a lot. The IQR uses only the middle 50%, so it hardly changes.

questions.prompt: Which graph is best for investigating whether two numerical variables are related?
questions.explanation: A scatter plot shows each pair of values as a point.

questions.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.right: Values that divide ordered data into four equal parts
A value far away from the rest of the data
Value below which a given percentage of the data lies

questions.explanation: These are the measures of dispersion in Grade 9.

questions.prompt: The 50th percentile is the same as the...
questions.explanation: Half the data lies below the median.

questions.prompt: In 15 matches a team scored 0 goals 3 times, 1 goal 5 times, 2 goals 4 times, 3 goals twice and 4 goals once. Calculate the mean number of goals per match, correct to two decimal places.
A broken-line graph is a good way to show how a quantity changes over time.
questions.explanation: Joining the points in time order shows increases and decreases clearly.

questions.prompt: For the data $12;\ 15;\ 17;\ 20;\ 22;\ 25;\ 28;\ 30$, find the median, the lower and upper quartiles, and the interquartile range.

The table shows the number of siblings of 20 learners.
Siblings: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Learners: 2, 6, 7, 3, 2
Calculate the mean number of siblings.

Look at the scatter plot of hours studied against test mark in the notes.
(a) Describe the correlation.  (1)
(b) Estimate the mark of a learner who studies for 6 hours.  (1)
(c) Does the graph prove that studying longer causes higher marks? Explain.  (1)
questions.memo:
(a) Positive correlation ✓ (1)
(b) About 65% to 70% ✓ (1)
(c) No: correlation does not prove cause; other factors also affect marks ✓ (1)

questions.prompt:
The ages of people at a party are $5;\ 6;\ 6;\ 7;\ 8;\ 9;\ 40$.
(a) Identify the outlier.  (1)
(b) Calculate the mean with and without the outlier.  (2)
(c) Which measure, the mean or the median, better describes a typical age? Explain.  (1)
questions.memo:
(a) $40$ ✓ (1)
(b) With: $81 \div 7 \approx 11{,}57$ ✓; without: $41 \div 6 \approx 6{,}83$ ✓ (2)
(c) The median ($7$), because the outlier pulls the mean up ✓ (1)
